title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning for Business AI
summary: Choose between retrieving source material and changing learned response behavior by identifying the failure you need to fix.
answer: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies relevant material at answer time. Fine-tuning adapts model behavior using training examples. Start by separating missing knowledge from inconsistent task behavior; a system can need either or both.
rows: Main job
Bring relevant source passages into the current request.
Adapt a model’s behavior from examples.
Changing business facts
Update the approved collection and retrieval process.
Do not assume training updates will keep changing facts current.
Evidence review
Inspect retrieved passages and their versions.
Evaluate behavior against held-out examples.
Typical failure
Relevant evidence is absent, inaccessible, or poorly ranked.
Training examples fail to represent the production task.
scenario: A policy assistant answers from outdated documents and also ignores the required response format. First fix source authority and retrieval to address stale answers. Then test whether instructions and examples solve the formatting problem before considering training. One intervention should not be credited for a different problem.
steps: Label recent failures as missing knowledge, bad retrieval, instruction failure, format failure, or incorrect reasoning.
Build separate tests for finding evidence and using it correctly.
Trial the least complex change that addresses the dominant failure.
Compare accepted quality and maintenance effort before choosing a combined design.
test: Change a policy’s effective date in the approved source. Check that the system uses the new passage and preserves the required format. A correctly formatted answer containing an old policy still fails.
trap: Treating fine-tuning as a convenient substitute for a current, permissioned source of business facts.

title: Keyword vs Semantic vs Hybrid Search for AI Knowledge Bases
summary: Choose retrieval methods with a query set that includes exact identifiers, paraphrases, and questions that should return no answer.
answer: Keyword search is useful for exact terms and identifiers. Semantic search compares meaning. Hybrid retrieval combines signals. Choose with measured retrieval quality on your collection rather than assuming one approach wins for every question.
rows: Exact identifiers
Test product codes, clause labels, and internal abbreviations.
Preserve exact-match behavior when meaning-based ranking is added.
Paraphrased questions
May need synonyms or query expansion.
Can surface conceptually similar passages with different wording.
Evaluation unit
Relevant documents and passages in the returned set.
The same relevant documents and passages, using the same test cases.
Operational constraint
Keep permissions and document freshness correct.
Keep permissions and freshness correct across every retrieval stage.
scenario: A support collection contains a product called AX-14 and a policy called expedited replacement. One user searches AX-14; another asks how to get a replacement faster. A useful search system must handle both without confusing AX-14 with AX-41 or retrieving a superseded policy.
steps: Collect representative exact, paraphrased, ambiguous, and unanswerable queries.
Have reviewers identify the passages that would support a correct answer.
Compare retrieval methods on those passages before evaluating generated prose.
Inspect failures by query type and choose a design that meets the task’s acceptance criteria.
test: Use two products with nearly identical names and conflicting policies. Confirm the retrieved passage belongs to the correct product and version. Then paraphrase a valid question and repeat the check.
trap: Judging retrieval by a fluent answer instead of checking whether the right evidence was retrieved.

title: Batch vs Real-Time AI Processing
summary: Match the processing mode to the business deadline, retry behavior, and how users receive the finished result.
answer: Use asynchronous batch processing when independent jobs can wait and completion is tracked separately. Use an interactive path when a person needs a response during the current task. A mixed system can prioritize urgent work and process the remainder later.
rows: User expectation
A job is submitted and a result is collected later.
A response arrives while the user is waiting.
Work organization
Track each request by a stable identifier.
Track each interaction and any background continuation.
Failure handling
Reconcile missing, failed, and completed items independently.
Show timeouts and give the user a clear recovery option.
Decision criterion
Allowed delay, completion handling, and total operating cost.
Required response time, quality, and peak capacity.
scenario: An operations team classifies a nightly backlog of closed tickets and also drafts answers for agents working live. The nightly analysis can run asynchronously. The draft assistant needs a separate response-time target; treating both as the same queue makes the user experience unpredictable.
steps: Write the latest useful completion time for each task category.
Give every item a stable ID and an explicit completed, failed, or pending state.
Test partial completion and retries before sending a large backlog.
Compare total cost and time to accepted output for the appropriate processing mode.
test: Submit a set containing valid requests and one malformed item. The reconciliation should preserve valid results, identify the failed item, and avoid replaying successful external actions.
trap: Assuming that submission means completion or that an entire batch must be repeated when one item fails.
source_label: OpenAI Batch documentation; verify current limits and terms before implementation

title: Prompt Engineering vs Context Engineering
summary: Distinguish instructions from the evidence, tools, state, and memory surrounding a business AI task.
answer: Prompt engineering focuses on the instructions and examples for a task. Context engineering considers the wider information available during a run. When a correct instruction is paired with irrelevant or stale evidence, improving only the instruction may leave the failure unchanged.
rows: Primary question
What task and output should the model produce?
What information and tools should be available now?
Typical artifact
Instructions, examples, and response requirements.
Source selection, retrieval rules, state, and tool interfaces.
Failure to inspect
Ambiguous instructions or inconsistent examples.
Missing evidence, conflicting documents, or stale state.
Test discipline
Hold the context constant when comparing prompts.
Hold the task constant when comparing source and state strategies.
scenario: A customer brief assistant follows the requested format but uses notes from the wrong account. A longer instruction does not fix the account selection bug. The team needs a verified customer identifier, current account evidence, and a clear distinction between retrieved material and operating instructions.
steps: Inspect the actual input bundle for a failed run.
Separate task instructions, evidence, tool outputs, and retained state.
Remove irrelevant or superseded information and verify source identity.
Test prompt and context changes independently so the cause of improvement is visible.
test: Give the assistant a current account note and a contradictory archived note. Confirm source authority is preserved and the archive does not silently override the current record.
trap: Appending every document to the request and expecting stronger instructions to resolve all contradictions.

title: Structured AI Outputs vs Free-Text Responses
summary: Use an output contract when another system needs fields, and retain a separate check for whether those fields are true.
answer: Structured output is useful when a workflow requires named fields and defined types. Free text gives an editor flexibility for narrative work. Format validity and factual correctness are separate acceptance checks, even when a provider supports schema-constrained generation.
rows: Downstream consumer
Software expecting known fields and types.
A person reviewing narrative content.
Validation
Schema checks plus business rules and evidence checks.
Editorial checklist plus business rules and evidence checks.
Missing evidence
Represent unknown explicitly with an allowed value.
Explain the gap without inventing a complete story.
Failure mode
Valid-looking fields with unsupported values.
Useful information hidden in inconsistent prose.
scenario: An invoice preparation workflow needs invoice ID, service period, and supporting source references. JSON with a valid date is still wrong if it came from a different invoice. The pipeline should validate the schema, confirm record identity, and reconcile source values before passing the output onward.
steps: Define the minimum fields the receiving system actually needs.
Specify types, allowed values, and how unknown information is represented.
Validate format separately from identity, evidence, and business constraints.
Test malformed input, ambiguous values, and valid-format incorrect answers.
test: Supply an invoice without a service date. The output should preserve a documented unknown rather than fabricate a plausible date to satisfy a required field.
trap: Equating schema compliance with an accurate business record.

title: Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent Business Systems
summary: Decide whether additional agents improve the work enough to justify coordination, cost, and new failure paths.
answer: A single agent is easier to trace when one task has a shared context and a clear tool set. Multiple agents can be useful for independently scoped work. Add agents only when their responsibilities, handoffs, and evaluation make the extra coordination worthwhile.
rows: Work boundaries
One task owner with a shared working context.
Explicitly separated subtasks with defined outputs.
Coordination
Fewer handoffs to inspect.
An orchestrator or process must reconcile results.
Evidence handling
Track sources across one run.
Preserve provenance across every handoff.
Comparison metric
Accepted output, latency, review effort, and cost.
The same metrics including coordination and reconciliation.
scenario: A research brief needs parallel reviews of three independent supplied document sets. Separate workers may help if each returns a source-linked evidence table. The final editor still needs to identify contradictory conclusions. Three agents repeating the same unsupported inference do not create three independent sources.
steps: Build a traceable single-agent or fixed-workflow baseline.
Identify subtasks that can be scoped and evaluated independently.
Define the output and evidence contract for every handoff.
Compare the full system, including reconciliation and failure recovery, against the baseline.
test: Give two workers source sets containing conflicting effective dates. The final system should surface the conflict and request the authority decision rather than settle it by majority vote.
trap: Treating agreement between models as independent evidence or assuming more agents guarantee a better answer.
